text: The National Fascist Party (Italian: Partito Nazionale Fascista, PNF) was established by Benito Mussolini as the political expression of Italian fascism and as a reorganisation of the previous Italian Fasces of Combat. It ruled the Kingdom of Italy from 1922, following the March on Rome, until the fall of the Fascist regime in 1943, when Mussolini was deposed by the Grand Council of Fascism. The PNF was succeeded by the Republican Fascist Party in the territories under the Italian Social Republic and was ultimately dissolved at the end of World War II. Rooted in Italian nationalism and the desire to restore and expand Italian territories, the party believed such expansion was necessary for national superiority and to avoid decay. Italian Fascists claimed modern Italy was the heir to ancient Rome and supported the creation of an Italian Empire to provide spazio vitale ("living space") for Italian settlers and to control the Mediterranean Sea. The party promoted a corporatist economic system in which employer and employee syndicates formed associations to represent economic producers and collaborate with the state in setting national economic policy, aiming to resolve class conflict through cooperation. It also strongly advocated autarky. Italian Fascism opposed liberalism and Marxist socialism due to their opposition to nationalism, and rejected reactionary conservatism as espoused by Joseph de Maistre, instead advocating respect for tradition and a shared Italian past alongside modernisation and a vision of Italy as the hegemonic power in Europe. The PNF and its successor, the Republican Fascist Party, are the only parties banned from re-formation by the Italian Constitution, which states that re-organisation of the dissolved Fascist party is forbidden under any form. After World War I, Italian nationalism claimed Italy was cheated in the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye (1919), particularly over the loss of Fiume (Rijeka) to Yugoslavia and exclusion from the wartime Treaty of London (1915), which had promised territorial gains for Italy. In September 1919, war hero Gabriele D'Annunzio established the Italian Regency of Carnaro, promulgating the Carta del Carnaro, a syncretic blend of right-wing and left-wing ideas that influenced early Italian fascism. The Regency was deposed in December 1920 after the Treaty of Rapallo. The PNF was founded in Rome during the Third Fascist Congress on 7–10 November 1921, marking the transformation of the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento into a political party. The party played a key role in promoting Mussolini's ideology, with Blackshirts (squadristi) gaining support from landowners by violently attacking socialists and their institutions in the rural Po Valley. On 28 October 1922, Mussolini attempted a coup known as the March on Rome, involving nearly 30,000 fascists, led by quadrumvirs General Emilio De Bono, Italo Balbo, Michele Bianchi, and Cesare Maria de Vecchi, with Mussolini remaining behind and allowing himself to be photographed marching. Generals Gustavo Fara and Sante Ceccherini assisted in preparations, and other organisers included Marquis Dino Perrone Compagni and Ulisse Igliori. On 24 October 1922, Mussolini declared before 60,000 people in Naples: "Our program is simple: we want to rule Italy." Blackshirts had already taken control of the Po plain and key strategic points. On 26 October, former prime minister Antonio Salandra warned current prime minister Luigi Facta of Mussolini's demands, but Facta did not believe the threat and thought Mussolini would govern quietly. Facta ordered a state of siege for Rome, but King Victor Emmanuel III refused to sign the military order. On 30 October, the King handed power to Mussolini, who was supported by the military, business class, and right-wing population. The march involved fewer than 30,000 men, and the King feared civil war due to the fascists' control of the country. Mussolini was asked to form his cabinet on 31 October 1922, with around 25,000 Blackshirts parading in Rome, and thus legally attained power under the Statuto Albertino. The March on Rome was not a conquest but a constitutional transfer of power enabled by the surrender of public authorities to fascist intimidation. Many business leaders believed they could manipulate Mussolini, who initially emphasized free market and laissez-faire economics, but this proved optimistic as his corporatist model granted the state total control over businesses through industry bodies ("corporations"), with businesses retaining property rights but few freedoms. After the coup, a parallel agreement was reached between Mussolini and King Victor Emmanuel III, leading to Mussolini becoming head of government. On 15 December, the Grand Council of Fascism was founded as the supreme organ of the PNF. After modifying electoral legislation with the Acerbo Law, the Fascist Party won the controversial April 1924 elections. In early 1925, Mussolini abandoned democracy and established a total dictatorship, making the PNF the only legally permitted party in Italy, a status formalised by a 1928 law and maintained until 1943. This shift was strongly criticised by Giacomo Matteotti, whose speech in Parliament led to his kidnapping and murder by fascist blackshirts. The regime imposed Fascist ideology and symbols nationwide, requiring party membership for employment or government assistance, displaying fasces in public buildings, and promoting a personality cult around Mussolini as "Il Duce." The Italian parliament was replaced by the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations, filled exclusively with PNF members. The party promoted Italian imperialism in Africa and racial segregation and white supremacy in colonies. In 1930, the Youth Fasces of Combat were established. In the 1930s, secretary Achille Starace, a loyalist from Southern Italy, launched a campaign of ceremonies, rallies, and youth organisations to shape national and personal identity. Starace brought the Opera Nazionale Balilla (ONB) under PNF control and dissolved the Youth Fasces, merging them into the Gioventù Italiana del Littorio (GIL). On 27 May 1933, party membership became required for public office; on 9 March 1937, it became mandatory for all public office holders; and from 3 June 1938, non-members were barred from working. In 1939, Ettore Muti replaced Starace, reflecting the increasing influence of Galeazzo Ciano, Mussolini’s son-in-law and Minister of Foreign Affairs. On 10 June 1940, from the balcony of Palazzo Venezia, Mussolini announced Italy's entry into World War II on the side of Nazi Germany. On 25 July 1943, following Dino Grandi's request due to war failures, the Grand Council of Fascism overthrew Mussolini, asking King Victor Emmanuel III to restore full authority and remove Mussolini as prime minister, which he did. Mussolini was imprisoned, the Fascist organisations collapsed, and the party was officially banned by Pietro Badoglio's government on 27 July. After the Nazi-engineered Gran Sasso raid liberated Mussolini in September, the PNF was revived as the Republican Fascist Party (Partito Fascista Repubblicano – PFR) on 13 September, as the sole party of the Northern Italian Social Republic (the Salò Republic), with Alessandro Pavolini as secretary. The PFR did not outlast Mussolini's execution and the collapse of the Salò state in April 1945, during the final Allied offensive in Italy. Italian Fascism was based on Italian nationalism and Georges Sorel's revolutionary syndicalism, evolving into national syndicalism, with many revolutionary syndicalist leaders becoming founders of the movement and holding key positions in Mussolini’s administration. The movement sought to restore and expand Italian territories to assert national strength and avoid decay, claiming modern Italy inherited Roman and Renaissance legacies and promoted the cultural identity of Romanitas ("Roman-ness"). It viewed ancient Rome as the "First Rome" and Renaissance Italy as the "Second Rome," with Mussolini emulating Julius Cæsar and Augustus. The Doctrine of Fascism (1932), ghostwritten by Giovanni Gentile, declared the Fascist state as a will to power and empire, with empire being both territorial and spiritual, guiding other nations without conquest. The regime promoted the restoration of the Mazzinian Risorgimento, claiming it had been abandoned in Giolittian-era Italy, and sought to incorporate "unredeemed" territories. To the east, the Fascists claimed Dalmatia as Italian due to its historical Italian cultural roots, including Venetian influence, and supported the return of Italians of Dalmatian heritage, especially after the 1919 revocation of the Treaty of London's promise to include Dalmatia. The regime supported the annexation of Slovenia into Italy, resulting in a quarter of Slovene ethnic territory and approximately 327,000 out of 1.3 million Slovenes being subjected to forced Italianization. It claimed Albania as Italian due to historical links with Illyrian and Roman populations, Roman and Venetian influence, and the presence of hundreds of thousands of Albanians in southern Italy, and endorsed assimilation and colonization of Albania with Italian settlers. The regime also claimed the Ionian Islands as Italian, citing their Venetian ownership from the mid-14th to the 18th century. To the west of Italy, the regime pursued similar imperial ambitions.

Albania was claimed by the Fascist regime as ethnically linked to Italy through prehistoric Italiotes, Illyrian, and Roman populations, with Roman and Venetian imperial influence justifying Italy's right to possess it. The regime also argued that hundreds of thousands of Albanians had been absorbed into Southern Italy, making the incorporation of Albania a reasonable step to unite people of Albanian descent. It endorsed Albanian irredentism, particularly targeting Kosovo and Epirus, especially the Chameria region with a significant Albanian population. After annexing Albania in 1939, the regime promoted assimilating Albanians into Italian culture and colonizing the country with Italian settlers from the Italian Peninsula to transform it into Italian territory. The Fascists claimed the Ionian Islands as Italian due to their historical possession by the Venetian Republic from the mid-14th to the 18th century. To the west, they asserted that Corsica, Nice, and Savoy belonged to Italy, citing historical, ethnic, and linguistic grounds. This claim stemmed from the 1860–1861 Italian unification, when Piedmont-Sardinia, under Count Cavour, was pressured by French Emperor Napoleon III to cede Nice and Savoy in exchange for French support of unification. The Fascist regime produced literature on Corsica and Nice, citing Petrarch’s statement that "the border of Italy is the Var; consequently Nice is a part of Italy" and Giuseppe Garibaldi’s assertion that "Corsica and Nice must not belong to France," claiming they would one day be reclaimed. Mussolini initially pursued Corsican annexation through encouraging autonomist movements and independence before annexation. To the north, the regime in the 1930s sought to annex Ticino and Graubünden in Switzerland, arguing that Romansch was an Italian dialect and that Graubünden should be incorporated into Italy. In November 1938, Mussolini declared to the Grand Fascist Council that Italy would extend its border to the Gotthard Pass. The regime accused Switzerland of oppressing the Romansch people and claimed Ticino due to its historical belonging to the Duchy of Milan until 1515, and areas in Graubünden, such as the Mesolcina and Hinterrhein, were held by the Milanese Trivulzio family. In 1940, Galeazzo Ciano proposed to Hitler and Ribbentrop the division of Switzerland along the central Western Alps, including Valais. To the south, the regime claimed Malta, which had been under British control since 1800, arguing that Maltese was an Italian dialect and that Malta was the cradle of Latin civilization; Italian had been an official language until 1937, when it was abolished by the British after Italy invaded Ethiopia. Italian irredentists claimed North African coastal territories as Italy’s Fourth Shore, citing Roman rule as justification. In January 1939, Italy annexed Libya’s coastal provinces—Tripoli, Misurata, Benghazi, and Derna—into metropolitan Italy, granting indigenous Libyans the right to apply for "Special Italian Citizenship" requiring literacy in Italian and valid only in Libya. Tunisia, a French protectorate since 1881, was seen as a loss to Italian ambitions, and upon entering WWII, Italy declared its intent to seize Tunisia and Algeria’s Constantine province. Italy also sought to annex Portugal’s colonies in the 1920s, viewing Portugal as weak and poorly managing its colonies, though relations were influenced by Salazar’s authoritarian, nationalist regime aligned with Britain. In 1925, the PNF declared the Fascist state to be totalitarian, initially a term used pejoratively by liberals, which the Fascists redefined positively as a state that unifies all values and creates politically active citizens. The Doctrine of Fascism (1932) stated that for the fascist, everything is in the state, and no human or spiritual value exists outside it, defining fascism as totalitarian. H. R. Knickerbocker noted in 1941 that Mussolini’s regime was the least terroristic among totalitarian states, citing mild treatment of a dissenting journalist, in contrast to Soviet or Nazi torture and execution. However, historians note extreme violence in Italian colonies: one-tenth of Libya’s population died during the Fascist era from gassings, concentration camps, starvation, and disease, and a quarter of a million Ethiopians died during and after the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. Italian Fascism promoted a corporatist economy with employer and employee syndicates working with the state to set national economic policy, criminalizing strikes and lockouts as harmful to national unity. The political anthem was "Giovinezza" ("The Youth"), emphasizing youth as a critical period for moral development. The regime promoted "moral hygiene" of youth, condemning homosexuality as deviant, criminalizing birth control and abortion, taxing bachelors, and viewing pre-pubertal male sexual excitement as a cause of criminality. It launched aggressive campaigns to reduce young women’s prostitution. Mussolini viewed women’s primary role as childbearers, stating "war is to man what maternity is to the woman," and introduced financial incentives for large families, policies to reduce female employment, and ceremonies honoring women as "reproducers of the nation." In 1934, he declared that women’s work was incompatible with childbearing and that unemployment for men could be solved by women’s exit from the workforce. Fascism emphasized a shared past and modernized Italy, with Mussolini calling for art that was "traditionalist and at the same time modern, looking to the past and the future." Traditional Roman symbols, such as the fasces (symbolizing unity, authority, and power) and the she-wolf of Rome, were used to represent shared heritage. In 1926, the fasces was adopted as a state symbol, though a redesign of the national flag incorporating it was blocked by monarchists; instead, the tricolour was raised with a black Fascist flag. Later, after Mussolini’s 1943 rescue by German forces, the Italian Social Republic used a fasces-variant flag. Initially republican and anti-monarchical, Italian Fascism shifted in 1922 to recognize the monarchy as a necessary compromise to gain support, especially given King Victor Emmanuel III’s popularity after WWI and army loyalty. The regime publicly linked Victor Emmanuel II and other historical figures like Cavour, Garibaldi, and Julius Caesar to a tradition of dictatorship. Despite this, the relationship with the monarchy remained strained, with Mussolini reducing the King’s power by creating the position of First Marshal of the Empire in 1938, giving him equal military authority. Mussolini privately resented the monarchy, envying Hitler’s dual role as head of state and government, and planned to dismantle the monarchy and establish a republic upon Italian military success. After being deposed in 1943 and Italy switching to the Allies, Fascism returned to republicanism and condemned the monarchy. In his 1943 speech, Mussolini praised Hitler and condemned Victor Emmanuel III for betraying the regime, stating that "it is not the regime that has betrayed the monarchy, it is the monarchy that has betrayed the regime," and that a new national and social Fascist state would be established. The regime did not denounce the House of Savoy entirely, praising Victor Emmanuel II for rejecting dishonorable pacts and blaming Victor Emmanuel III for betraying him by joining the Allies. The relationship with the Catholic Church was initially anti-clerical but shifted in the 1920s as Mussolini sought cooperation. In 1929, the Lateran Treaty created Vatican City, ending decades of conflict after the 1870 annexation of the Papal States. Fascism justified its 1938 antisemitic laws by claiming they fulfilled the Catholic Church’s mandate from the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, which required Jews to wear distinctive clothing. Italian Fascism influenced global movements, with admiration from Winston Churchill, Sigmund Freud, George Bernard Shaw, and Thomas Edison for its law and order, and its anti-Mafia stance. It influenced Adolf Hitler’s Nazi Party, the Russian Fascist Organization, Brit HaBirionim, the British Union of Fascists, the Romanian National Fascist Movement, and the Sammarinese Fascist Party, which established a government in San Marino. In Yugoslavia, Milan Stojadinović founded the Yugoslav Radical Union, with members wearing green shirts, Šajkača caps, and using the Roman salute, and calling himself Vodja. In Switzerland, pro-Nazi Colonel Arthur Fonjallaz, after visiting Italy in 1932, became a strong Mussolini admirer and advocated for Italian annexation of Switzerland, receiving Fascist foreign aid. Switzerland hosted two Italian politico-cultural activities: the International Centre for Fascism.

George Bernard Shaw and Thomas Edison are mentioned in the context of a statement about the Fascist Government combating organised crime and the Mafia with violence and vendetta (honour), though this connection appears to be an error or misattribution, as no factual link between these individuals and the Fascist Government is supported by the document. Italian Fascism influenced Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party, the Russian Fascist Organization, Brit HaBirionim, the British Union of Fascists, the Romanian National Fascist Movement (including the National Romanian Fascia and the National Italo-Romanian Cultural and Economic Movement), and the Sammarinese Fascist Party, which established a government in San Marino based on essentially Italian Fascism. In the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, Milan Stojadinović founded the Yugoslav Radical Union, a Fascist party, with members wearing green shirts, Šajkača caps, and using the Roman salute; Stojadinović also referred to himself as Vodja. In Switzerland, pro-Nazi Colonel Arthur Fonjallaz of the National Front became a strong admirer of Mussolini after visiting Italy in 1932 and advocated for Italian annexation of Switzerland while receiving Fascist foreign aid. Switzerland hosted two Italian politico-cultural activities: the International Centre for Fascist Studies (CINEF — Centre International d'Études Fascistes) and the 1934 congress of the Action Committee for the Universality of Rome (CAUR — Comitato d'Azione della Università de Roma). In Spain, writer Ernesto Giménez Caballero, in his 1932 work Genio de España (The Genius of Spain), called for Italian annexation of Spain under Mussolini leading an international Latin Catholic empire, but later became closely associated with Falangism, resulting in the abandonment of the annexation idea. In India, Italian Fascism, particularly the Opera Nazionale Balilla, influenced B.S. Moonje and the Hindu Mahasabha. In Brazil, Italian Fascism inspired and financed Plínio Salgado's Brazilian Integralist Action. Although the National Fascist Party was outlawed by Italy's postwar Constitution, several neo-fascist parties emerged to continue its legacy. Historically, the largest neo-fascist party was the Italian Social Movement (Movimento Sociale Italiano), which achieved its best electoral result with 8.7% of the vote in the 1972 general election. The MSI was disbanded in 1995 and replaced by National Alliance, a conservative party that distanced itself from Fascism, as its founder, former foreign minister Gianfranco Fini, stated during an official visit to the State of Israel that Fascism was "an absolute evil." National Alliance and other neo-fascist parties were merged in 2009 to form the short-lived People of Freedom party led by then Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, which eventually dissolved after the defeat in the 2013 general election. Many former members of the MSI and National Alliance later joined Brothers of Italy, including Giorgia Meloni, Ignazio La Russa, Adolfo Urso, Francesco Lollobrigida, Daniela Santanchè, Luca Ciriani, Tommaso Foti, Nello Musumeci, Gianni Alemanno, Giovanni Donzelli, Nicola Procaccini, Andrea Delmastro Delle Vedove, Marcello Gemmato, Paola Frassinetti, Galeazzo Bignami, Claudio Barbaro, Isabella Rauti, Wanda Ferro, Edmondo Cirielli, Giovanbattista Fazzolari, Alessio Butti, Francesco Acquaroli, Marco Marsilio, Federico Mollicone, Romano Maria La Russa, Marcello Taglialatela, and Michele Rallo.
